sections.overview: The Eurasian wryneck is an unusual woodpecker that rarely climbs trees. It is named for its snake-like way of twisting its head, and it is the only European woodpecker to migrate over long distances.
sections.identification: A slim bird 16–18 cm long, weighing about 33 g, with a wing near 90 mm. The plumage is delicately patterned in grey, brown and buff, with a dark band running from the nape onto the back and arrowhead-shaped marks on the creamy underparts. The bill is short and less dagger-like than other woodpeckers’.
sections.habitat: It is mainly a bird of grassland and open country. In Britain it was once found on commons, heathland, orchards, parkland and larger gardens of central and southern England, and it nests in existing holes, wall crevices, banks or nest boxes.
sections.diet: It eats almost entirely ants, which it collects on the ground, along with beetles and their larvae, moths, spiders and woodlice. It catches prey with its tongue and forages mostly by hopping on the ground with the tail raised.
sections.behavior: Unlike other woodpeckers it seldom climbs trunks. It can turn its head nearly 180 degrees, and when disturbed at the nest its neck twists in all directions while it hisses; this snake-like display is thought to deter predators. It sometimes feigns death.
sections.reproduction: It uses no nesting material. A clutch is typically 7–10 eggs (observed 5–12), incubated for 12–14 days, mainly by the female. The naked, helpless chicks fledge after 18–22 days, and there is usually one brood. Breeding typically starts at one year of age.
sections.ecology: The wryneck depends on ant supplies and on ready-made cavities and crevices, as it builds no nest of its own. It migrates to tropical Africa and to southern Asia from Iran to the Indian subcontinent, and passes through Britain in spring and autumn.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern; the world population is estimated at up to 15 million and may be declining slightly. In Britain it has been lost as a breeder: the last confirmed breeding record was in 2002, and it is now a scarce passage migrant, mostly seen in August and September.
